books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Special Message to Congress, May 11, 1846

stimulus.source_note: James K. Polk, Special Message to Congress, May 11, 1846. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Upon the earnest appeal both of the Congress and convention of Texas I had ordered an efficient military force to take a position “between the Nueces and the Del Norte.”

Mexico has passed the boundary of the United States, has invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil. She has proclaimed that hostilities have commenced, and that the two nations are now at war.

As war exists, and, notwithstanding all our efforts to avoid it, exists by the act of Mexico herself, we are called upon by every consideration of duty and patriotism to vindicate with decision the honor, the rights, and the interests of our country.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A historian who doubts Polk's account would most likely point out which of the following?

options.text: Polk ordered American troops into the disputed strip before any fighting, then called the clash an invasion.
Mexico had already accepted the Rio Grande as the border of Texas before 1846.
options.misconception: Mexico never accepted the Rio Grande line; it insisted the border was the Nueces River.

options.text: Congress refused to declare war, so Polk fought the war without its approval.
options.misconception: Congress declared war on May 13, 1846, two days after Polk's message.

options.text: Texas had never been part of Mexico, so Mexico had no claim to any of its land.
options.misconception: Texas had been a Mexican province until its revolt in 1836, and Mexico never recognized its independence.

rationales.A: Taylor's army sat in the disputed strip on Polk's orders, so the clash happened on ground both sides claimed.
rationales.B: Mexico held to the Nueces as the border all along; accepting the Rio Grande would have given up the strip.
rationales.C: Congress did declare war, on May 13, 1846, two days after the message.
rationales.D: Texas was a Mexican province until 1836, and Mexico never recognized the Lone Star Republic.
rationales.general:
1. Start with what Polk does not say: his own order put the army in the disputed strip first.
2. Add the two border claims. The ground where blood was shed was claimed by both countries, not clearly American.
3. Put the pieces together. A president who marches into disputed land can then call the fight an invasion.
Remember: a claim that someone else started it always deserves one question: who walked onto the disputed ground first?
